paragraph.text: G19. "Veganism is an eating disorder in disguise"

eating disorders are serious illnesses, and there is indeed a statistical association between them and meat-free diets. But the best-documented direction is the reverse: people who already have a disorder sometimes adopt vegetarianism as a socially accepted way of restricting food. In a community sample, vegans showed no more signs of disordered eating than omnivores. When a vegan falls ill or dies of an eating disorder, it's a tragedy caused by the illness, not by the ethics of not exploiting animals.
if you or someone close to you shows signs of an eating disorder, seek professional help. The subject is handled here with care, because it involves real suffering
"That's not ethics, it's an eating disorder. Did you see that vegan who died? It was veganism."
Studies find more vegetarians and vegans among people with eating disorders than in the general population.
Diets that exclude whole food groups encourage food restriction.
Cases of vegans who fell ill or died from eating disorders show this risk.
So veganism is, or causes, an eating disorder, not an ethical choice.

P1 is true, and it's important to acknowledge it. P2 has some truth for people who already have a disorder. The problem lies in the conclusion, which confuses correlation with cause and treats tragic cases as the rule.
: from a statistical association it doesn't follow that veganism causes the disorder, nor that every vegan has one.
"It's an eating disorder disguised as ethics."
"Another vegan starved to death. How long will people keep defending this?"
"Restrictive diets adopted for moral reasons can mask eating pathology."
"I know someone who got sick being vegan." (which is G10)

Some people get ill and become very afraid of eating, and that's a serious illness that needs a doctor. Sometimes those people say they don't eat meat, but the problem is the illness, not the meat. Being vegan is something else: it's not wanting animals to suffer, and eating well, with beans, rice, fruit and lots of tasty things.

Eating disorders are serious illnesses and deserve care. Research shows that many people who already have a disorder start avoiding meat as a way of restricting food, not the other way around. In a community sample, vegans showed no more signs of disordered eating than omnivores. When someone falls ill or dies, the cause is the illness, which also affects many people who eat meat.
"If a person with anorexia avoids bread, would you say bread caused the anorexia?"

text.bold: 1. The best-documented direction is the reverse.

paragraph.text: In a study of women who had an eating disorder, most of those who became vegetarian said it was related to the disorder and began after it. In other words, the disorder came first, and the meat-free diet served as an accepted way to restrict.

A systematic review of 20 studies found an association between vegetarianism and eating disorders in young people, but stresses that, because the studies are cross-sectional, a causal link can't be established.

text.bold: 3. Vegans in the community don't show more signs of disorder.

paragraph.text: In a study of 578 people, vegans scored slightly lower than omnivores on a standard questionnaire of eating pathology. The differences were small, but pointed to slightly healthier attitudes toward food.

Avoiding meat to lose weight is different from avoiding animal products so as not to exploit animals. In the patient study, weight-related motivation appeared among those with a disorder, and not among those without one. That's why health professionals are advised to look into the reason for the diet.

text.bold: 5. Eating disorders affect every kind of diet.

paragraph.text: Anorexia has one of the highest mortality rates among mental disorders, and the vast majority of those affected aren't vegan. When a vegan dies of an eating disorder, the cause is the illness. Using someone's death to attack an ethical position is disrespectful to the victim and to others who suffer from the same illness.

text.bold: 6. Any diet can become a tool for restriction.

paragraph.text: Weight-loss diets, low carb, "clean eating" and fasting can also be used to restrict. No one concludes that all of them are disorders.
Women with an eating disorder history were more likely to have ever been vegetarian (52% vs 12%); most (68%) perceived their vegetarianism as related to the disorder and emerging after its onset

text.italic: Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics

paragraph.text: Systematic review of 20 studies: vegetarianism is associated with eating disorders, but the cross-sectional design prevents concluding cause
Among 578 people, vegans scored lower than omnivores on the EDE-Q, a measure of eating pathology; small differences
People with anorexia have mortality about six times higher than expected
(d) The strongest counter-reply: veganism provides cover for restriction

The most serious version says: even if veganism doesn't cause disorders, it offers a socially accepted justification for restricting food. Someone prone to a disorder would find in vegan discourse an excuse that's hard to question.
(e) Why the counter-reply doesn't reach the conclusion

text.bold: That calls for clinical attention, not rejecting the ethics.

paragraph.text: Professionals can look into the motivation for the diet and treat the disorder. That doesn't make animal exploitation just.
Health, appearance, religion and food intolerances are also used this way. Misuse doesn't invalidate the original reason.
Advocating a varied, sufficient vegan diet, not a restrictive one, protects those who are vulnerable.

Even if some people with eating disorders use veganism as cover, the question remains the same: is it just to breed and kill animals that feel? Caring for people with eating disorders and respecting animals aren't conflicting goals.

paragraph.text: And still attributes them to veganism when the patient is vegan.
Tragic cases of vegans stick in memory

Treating the ethics as illness eases the feeling of being judged
The principle being tested is: "if a diet is associated with a disorder, the diet is the cause and its motivation is illness".
Whoever avoids gluten or lactose would be mentally ill

It's right that eating disorders are serious illnesses with high mortality, and that there's a real association between them and meat-free diets. Health professionals do well to look into why a person with a disorder adopts a restrictive diet, and vegans do well to advocate a varied, sufficient diet, never restriction.

But association isn't cause, the best-documented direction is the reverse, and vegans in general don't show more signs of disorder. Respecting animals and caring for those who suffer from an eating disorder go together.
